gloss.text: Nimbostratus is the meteorologists’ name for the thick grey layer of cloud that brings steady rain or snow (Latin nimbus, rain cloud, and stratus, spread out); praecipitatio, “falling”, is the name for rain or snow that reaches the ground.
A coinage for the book, in the form of a scientific name: argillite (from Greek árgillos, clay), the slaty bedrock of Cambridge (Latin Cantabrigia).
Latin, “the days of the little dog”: the hot weeks when Sirius, the Dog Star (Canicula), rises with the sun.
Latin, “the tears of Saint Lawrence”: the Perseids peak about 12 August, close to his feast day on the 10th, and the meteors have long been called his tears.
A coinage for the book: Latin, “the first hoarfrost”.

The World Meteorological Organization’s term, from Russian, for a thin, elastic crust of new ice, up to 10 centimetres thick, that bends without breaking. It is a sea-ice word, borrowed here for the ponds.

Latin, “the equation of time”: the difference, through the year, between the clock and the sun. Because of it the earliest sunset comes about two weeks before the solstice, and the latest sunrise about two weeks after.
Seneca, “these sustain us”: corn, beans and squash, the three sisters, as Arthur C. Parker gave the word in 1910.
The asteroid whose dust makes the Geminids, found in 1983 and named for Phaethon, who in Greek myth drove the sun’s chariot too near the earth. It may be the burnt-out core of a comet.
From the first notice of the count, in Bird-Lore for December 1900, which proposed “a Christmas bird-census”. It has been held every winter since.
Latin, from sol, the sun, and sistere, to stand still: the word “solstice” comes from it.
Persian, “the night of Yalda”: the longest night of the year, kept in Iran and far beyond on the eve of the winter solstice, with pomegranates, watermelon and readings from Hafez.
Old English, “marsh, mud, dirt”: one of the oldest wetland words, reaching back through Proto-Germanic *fanja-, “swamp, marsh”, to the Proto-Indo-European root *pen-, “swamp”.
